# Interview kit (generated by scripts/build_phase9_docs.py; every number comes from a generated report)

Rules for using this kit: say "synthetic" in the first sentence you speak about results; never say the project "detects GenAI fraud";
if you quote a number, it must match `README_V2.md` on your own regenerated reports.

## 1. Two-minute demo script

| Time | Say / do |
|---|---|
| 0:00 | "This is a layered fraud-risk prototype on synthetic data. It scores a payment session and returns allow, review or block with an explanation. I rebuilt my hackathon version after finding flaws in my own evaluation." |
| 0:20 | Open `/api/v2/status` (the free plan sleeps, so open it before the demo; the deployed API must be redeployed with the Phase 7 code, otherwise run the demo locally). Point out the model version and that the API says it is synthetic. |
| 0:35 | Score `v2_sample_deepfake_kyc.json` at `/api/v2/dossier`. Read the headline, then the drivers, then the evidence flags. "The drivers explain the model; the flags are readable checks I wrote; they are different on purpose." |
| 1:05 | Score `v2_sample_ai_scripted_app.json`. It lands just under the review threshold and is allowed. "This is a near miss. I show it because it is honest about where the model stops." Read the actual numbers from the response. |
| 1:25 | Show the results table: v1 headline F1 0.976, the original attacks under grouped folds 0.975, and the harder world 0.824. "Nothing moved until the world got harder. That is the finding." |
| 1:45 | "Unseen fraud families are mostly invisible to the supervised model (FAKE_MERCHANT 0%). Learning from mistakes did not clearly help. Next I would test the modelling method on a real public dataset with time-based splits." |

## 2. Resume bullets (check each against what you can defend; adjust wording to your resume's style)

- Built and served (FastAPI) a layered payment-fraud risk prototype on synthetic data: XGBoost, Isolation Forest and autoencoder novelty detectors, history-only graph features and a cost-based allow/review/block policy with per-case explanations.
- Audited my own hackathon evaluation: customer-grouped splits, in-fold threshold learning, history-only graph features and unseen-family tests. F1 stayed at 0.975 on the original synthetic attacks but fell to 0.824 on a harder synthetic world with adaptive attackers.
- Measured unseen-fraud risk with leave-one-family-out tests (supervised recall on a held-out family as low as 0%) and reported precision at an assumed 0.6% fraud rate (0.10) instead of the synthetic mix.

Say "served" or "deployed" for v2 only after you have redeployed the API with the v2 and Phase 7 code; until then say "runs locally and in the repo".

Shorter version (one line): "Layered fraud-risk prototype on synthetic data with unseen-fraud evaluation; audited and corrected the evaluation of my own v1."

## 4. Interview Q&A (answer in your own words; these are the facts and the honest framing)

1. **Does it detect GenAI fraud?** No. It has four simulated GenAI-era families (synthetic identity, fake merchant, deepfake-KYC telemetry, AI-scripted APP). They are my assumptions, not validated. The honest claim is a layered prototype with unseen-fraud evaluation on synthetic data.
2. **Your v1 had F1 0.976. Is v2 worse?** On the same attacks it is about the same (World A F1 0.975), so the customer overlap and in-fold tuning problems did not inflate the score much (single-stage F1 0.980 with v1 folds vs 0.981 grouped). The drop is in World B (0.824), where attackers adapt: F1 0.986 with no adaptive attackers, 0.774 when all adapt. The lesson: the simulator was easy, and I measured how easy.
3. **Why report precision at 0.6% prevalence?** Because the synthetic mixes are 24% (World A) and 29% (World B) fraud. At a realistic rate, precision depends on the false-positive rate: 0.103 [0.077, 0.141] in World B and 0.401 [0.273, 0.577] in World A. Those numbers use an assumed rate, not a measured one.
4. **Why did calibration hurt?** Brier scores: World B raw 0.069, sigmoid 0.086, isotonic 0.082. I did not investigate why. Plausible reasons are small data and raw scores that were already reasonable, but that is a hypothesis, so say so. I report it as a measured negative result.
5. **What was the graph leakage?** My first graph features used all traces, including future ones, which made World A look better. Replaying traces in time order removed it; World A went 0.975 -> 0.975. World B kept a small gain: 0.810 -> 0.824.
6. **How do you know serving matches training?** One shared feature extractor, history-only graph features, and tests: the extractor equals my v1 extractor on every real trace except the intentional failure-feature fix; replaying training traces through the scorer reproduces the training features; the numpy novelty models match scikit-learn to 1e-9.
7. **How are thresholds chosen?** By expected cost with assumed constants (L = 500.0, q = 0.9, c_r = 12.0, c_fp = 25.0, prevalence = 0.006, review_cap = 0.05), learned on inner out-of-fold scores only, then evaluated on outer folds. The constants are assumptions; the thresholds move when they change.
8. **Stacking vs XGBoost alone?** World B cost per 10k: stacked 11,901, XGBoost only 12,186, naive max 24,268, allow everything 30,000. Stacking helps little; naive max is much worse.
9. **What happens with an unseen fraud family?** Supervised recall is near zero for some (FAKE_MERCHANT 0%); novelty detectors help for others but raise false alarms. Novelty-aware stacking was not worth it: mean cost 27,955 vs 21,731.
10. **What does the feedback loop show?** Nothing reliable. Targeted retraining versus a same-size control was small, inconsistent and within noise; most misses are stealth attackers (94% of misses). I report it as a negative result.
11. **Biggest false-alarm source?** Genuine "new payee then pay" (28% flagged) and person-to-person sprees (8%): they look like scams. In production this is the friction-versus-fraud trade-off.
12. **Why World A and World B separately?** Pooling lets the model learn which simulator made the trace (legit-vs-legit AUC 0.997).
13. **What would you do with real data?** Time-based splits, label delay, a same-size control for any retraining, threshold stability checks, and a human-validated cost model.
14. **What is not production-ready?** No authentication or rate limiting, in-memory state on one worker, Stage 1 rules not in v2 serving, and everything trained on synthetic data.
15. **What are you most proud of?** Finding and publishing my own evaluation flaws, with the measured size of each, instead of defending the original number.

## 6. Do not say

- "Detects GenAI / deepfake fraud" (it scores simulated KYC telemetry, not images or video).
- "Production-ready", "state of the art", or any real-world accuracy.
- "Validated on real data" (it was a method check on one public dataset, not the same system; say exactly that).
- Any number you have not regenerated on your own machine.
